planting.note: Root stem cuttings with at least one node in chunky, well-drained aroid mix under warm, humid conditions, then give the climbing stems a moss pole or trellis.

directions: This uncommon Monstera selection grows noticeably slower than typical cultivars, opening narrow, lance-shaped juvenile leaves that broaden into deeply lobed, heart-shaped mature foliage with age. Keep it within a few feet of a bright east- or west-facing window and provide a sturdy pole so aerial roots can grip as the vine climbs past six feet. Let the top couple inches of potting mix dry before rewatering, and keep it away from cold drafts or sudden temperature swings that can stall its already gradual growth.

planting.note: Pot divisions or rooted offsets of this irregularly branching, candelabra-like form into fast-draining mineral cactus mix and set in a sunny window or bright porch.

directions: This oddly contorted form of the blue myrtle cactus produces blue-green ribbed stems that branch unevenly, giving each plant a quirky, one-of-a-kind silhouette rather than the orderly columns of the straight species. It grows slowly and tolerates long stretches of neglect, making it forgiving for distracted plant owners. Give it several hours of direct sun daily and water only after the mineral mix has dried completely through, since standing moisture around its roots invites rot quickly.

planting.note: Pot this twisting, ribbed columnar cactus in coarse, fast-draining mineral mix and place where it gets strong, direct light for a meaningful part of the day.

directions: A novelty selection of a Chilean coastal columnar cactus, this form twists its ribs into a tight corkscrew spiral as it grows, giving each stem a sculptural, almost hand-carved look that sets it apart from ordinary straight-growing cactus. Growth is slow, so expect a modest-sized specimen for several years before it reaches real height. Keep it in strong direct light and water sparingly, soaking only after the coarse mix has dried out fully, since this coastal desert species has little tolerance for soggy roots.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in chunky, well-drained aroid mix near a bright east- or west-facing window and provide a pole or trellis for climbing growth.

directions: Leaves on this variegated dragon-tail pothos emerge streaked and blotched with irregular white patches, and as a climbing specimen matures its foliage develops the deep slits and holes associated with the species. Place it within a few feet of bright indirect light to keep the white sections from scorching while still supporting enough chlorophyll for steady growth, and let the top couple inches of mix dry between waterings. A moss pole or trellis encourages larger, more deeply fenestrated leaves than a plant left to trail along the soil surface.

planting.note: Root two-node stem cuttings in damp sphagnum or a chunky, fast-draining mix under high humidity, since this miniature hoya establishes slowly.

directions: Thick, heart-shaped leaves on this Bornean hoya carry a dense, irregular dusting of silver over a dark green base, giving trailing stems a frosted appearance distinct from plainer krohniana forms. Clusters of small, sweetly fragrant white flowers can appear mainly in spring and summer once the plant is well established. Grow in bright, filtered light in a chunky, fast-draining mix and let the substrate dry out between waterings, since the fleshy leaves store moisture and rot readily if kept wet.

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in a chunky, fast-draining mix and hang or set the mature trailing vine where it receives strong, bright light.

directions: A hybrid with Hoya lacunosa among its parentage, this selection carries small, glossy leaves that stay green in lower light but flush red to orange along the edges and tips when given strong, bright exposure. Small clusters of fragrant white flowers appear intermittently through the year once the vine matures. Grow in a chunky, fast-draining mix and let it dry out substantially between waterings, since it tolerates underwatering far better than consistently damp roots.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in a chunky, fast-draining mix and hang the mature vine in a basket where it can trail freely.

directions: This trailing hoya carries thick, glossy, waxy leaves along cascading stems, giving it a textured, rope-like look in a hanging basket. Set it within a few feet of a bright window, since it flowers more reliably with ample indirect light than in dim corners. Let the mix dry out completely before watering again, since the fleshy leaves store moisture like a succulent and are prone to rot if kept consistently damp.
